title: Resolving Tooling Ejection Friction via Diamond Mold Polishing
my_role: I investigated the ejection drag marks with the tooling engineer and coordinated the surface polish adjustment.
problem: The injection-molded enclosure was sticking inside the tool cavity and not ejecting cleanly, causing minor surface dragging and pin stress marks on trial test shots.
context: Cheeko's enclosure has deep sidewalls with minimal draft angles to maintain a compact, friendly silhouette. If ejection force is too high, parts deform, cycle times spike, and cosmetic reject rates climb.
investigation: Looked into friction between the molded ABS/PC blend and the tool steel cavity wall. Examined draft angle measurements on the CAD model versus real steel, and checked ejector pin distribution balance.
people: I worked closely with our tooling partner and mechanical engineering lead.
hypotheses: Draft angle is slightly undersized on the rear cavity walls.
EDM spark erosion texture on tool surface created micro-undercuts causing vacuum drag during demolding.
Cooling cycle duration is uneven across thick-to-thin transitions.
action: Rather than modifying the steel geometry or cutting deeper draft angles (which would alter the external industrial design profile), we specified progressive diamond polishing (#800 to #1200 grit) along the ejection vector in the critical drag zones.
result: The molded parts demolded effortlessly without sticking or pin deformation. Cycle time stabilized and surface finish met cosmetic A-surface specifications.
principle: Mold surface finish can directly alter production kinematics, not just aesthetic appearance. A CAD model is very obedient; plastic isn't.
next_time: Specify draw polishing along the ejection direction in early DFM review notes prior to first tool cut.
why_decision_made: Polishing the existing steel avoided costly tooling re-machining and preserved the exact industrial design silhouette without delaying delivery milestones.
technical_depth: Deep dive into tool steel surface roughness (Ra values), micro-undercut friction, draft tolerance margins in ABS/PC, and mold release dynamics.
product_thinking: Protected the physical feel and compact proportions of the handheld device rather than compromising industrial design when manufacturing friction appeared.
business_impact: Avoided a 3-week tooling modification cycle and thousands of dollars in mold re-cutting costs.
cross_functional_work: Bridged industrial design expectations with tooling shop realities to reach an actionable mechanical compromise.
one_line_takeaway: A CAD model is very obedient. Plastic isn't. Surface polish is a mechanical lever, not just a cosmetic one.

title: Designing for Extreme Constraint: The 320×240 Screen Interface
my_role: I designed the visual hierarchy, typographic rules, and state transitions for the display.
problem: Modern mobile design patterns failed completely on a 2.4-inch 320×240 embedded display. Text was unreadable, multi-button navigation felt cluttered, and children were overwhelmed by visual noise.
context: Cheeko is intentionally not an iPad. The screen exists solely to confirm voice intent, provide emotional feedback, and anchor physical knob interaction—not to consume continuous screen time.
investigation: Tested various pixel densities, font sizes, color contrasts, and animation frame rates on physical TFT/IPS hardware under direct ambient sunlight and bedside lighting.
people: I worked with our embedded firmware engineer and conducted quick observation sessions with kids and parents.
hypotheses: Standard responsive mobile UI frameworks contain too much layout overhead for low-power microcontrollers.
Kids need glanceable character feedback (eyes, states, icons) rather than textual paragraphs.
High refresh animations cause SPI bus bandwidth bottlenecks and battery drain.
action: Stripped the interface down to high-contrast, bold geometry and 3 primary states: Listening, Thinking, and Expressing. Created a custom bitmap-optimized typography hierarchy and strict 8-pixel grid rules where every UI element serves an explicit function.
result: Memory footprint on the MCU dropped by 64%, frame rendering remained locked at smooth 30fps without tearing, and child usability tests showed immediate comprehension without reading assistance.
principle: The screen was only 320×240, so every element had to earn its space. True screen constraint forces product honesty.
next_time: Test typography rendering directly on raw hardware panels on day one rather than designing in high-res Figma first.
why_decision_made: Ensured the product remained a voice-and-tactile companion rather than morphing into another passive entertainment screen.
technical_depth: Optimized frame buffer sizes, SPI display transfer bandwidth, color palettes (16-bit RGB565), and micro-animation keyframing.
product_thinking: Subtractive product design: keeping kids present in the real room while giving them just enough digital reassurance.
business_impact: Enabled use of an ultra-cost-effective, durable embedded display while significantly extending device battery life.
cross_functional_work: Translated high-level child psychology principles into exact byte-budgeted sprite sheets for firmware implementation.
one_line_takeaway: The screen was only 320×240, so every element had to earn its space.

title: Physical Controls: Selecting Rotary Encoders over Touchscreens
my_role: I evaluated interaction ergonomics and finalized the physical control architecture.
problem: Early feedback indicated touchscreen navigation induced accidental touches, greasy screen smudges, and fragile glass failure risks in young hands.
context: For a child, turning a solid mechanical knob offers instant physical feedback and muscular intuition that a flat glass screen cannot match.
investigation: Tested continuous rotary potentiometers versus stepped incremental rotary encoders with integrated push-click switches across 10 prototype housings.
people: I worked with our industrial designer and mechanical prototyping vendor.
hypotheses: A stepped detent encoder gives clear tactile 'clicks' per item, preventing overshooting in menus.
A knurled rubberized outer ring provides superior grip for small hands with varying motor skills.
action: Selected a 20-detent incremental rotary encoder with custom knurled silicone overmold. Paired it with two oversized silicone dome buttons with distinct actuation forces (300g vs 150g) to prevent accidental activation.
result: Zero learning curve during user testing. Children immediately turned the dial and understood 1 click = 1 choice without looking directly at their fingers.
principle: Tactile affordances make software invisible. Physical friction can be a feature, not a bug.
next_time: Audit encoder shaft wobble tolerances earlier to avoid custom stabilization bushings.
why_decision_made: Physical dials are indestructible compared to capacitive touch panels and reinforce screen-free intentionality.
technical_depth: Debounce algorithm timing in microcontroller interrupts, rotary encoder detent torque curves, silicone durometer selection (60 Shore A).
product_thinking: Interaction design is not just visual; it's acoustic and haptic. The sound of a click builds trust.
business_impact: Reduced touch-sensor BOM costs and lowered field failure rates from cracked glass screens.
cross_functional_work: Coordinated between firmware debounce logic and mechanical shaft tolerance to ensure smooth tactile response.
one_line_takeaway: Small mechanical click. Massive leap in usability. Tactile controls make technology feel honest.

title: Voice AI in the Physical Room: Acoustic Isolation & Speaker Vibration
my_role: I tested audio cancellation artifacts and coordinated microphone silicone baffling with engineering.
problem: When the device speaker played audio responses, the microphone picked up internal casing vibrations, causing the voice AI to interrupt itself or misinterpret its own audio as user speech.
context: Voice AI hardware is fundamentally constrained by acoustics. If the microphone hears the internal speaker vibration through the plastic chassis, acoustic echo cancellation (AEC) algorithms fail.
investigation: Analyzed microphone frequency response graphs during speaker playback at 70dB SPL. Dissected the enclosure to track acoustic leakage paths through screw bosses and split lines.
people: I worked with our acoustic consultant and hardware engineering team.
hypotheses: Vibration is conducting through the rigid plastic chassis directly into the MEMS microphone solder pads.
Acoustic port seal on the microphone boot is leaking sound from inside the enclosure chamber.
action: Designed a custom dual-cavity silicone rubber boot that physically decouples the MEMS mic from the PCB and plastic housing. Separated the speaker chamber with an airtight ultrasonic gasket.
result: Speaker-to-mic mechanical coupling dropped by 24dB. Acoustic echo cancellation locked in reliably, enabling clean barge-in and wake-word detection even during energetic storytelling.
principle: Voice AI does not live in the cloud; it lives in the physical acoustics of plastic, air, and rubber gaskets.
next_time: Enforce sealed acoustic chamber architecture in the primary CAD master model before any PCB layout begins.
why_decision_made: Essential for natural conversational voice UX: a conversational companion that talks over you or can't hear you is unusable.
technical_depth: MEMS microphone sealing, acoustic impedance, silicone durometer vibration dampening, SPL measurement, and digital signal processing (AEC/beamforming).
product_thinking: High-level AI prompts mean nothing if the physical microphone is deafened by plastic vibrations.
business_impact: Avoided having to add expensive dual-mic DSP co-processors by solving the problem mechanically.
cross_functional_work: Aligned acoustic physics with industrial design aesthetics to keep microphone pinholes clean and unobtrusive.
one_line_takeaway: Voice AI does not live in the cloud; it lives in the acoustic reality of plastic, air, and rubber.

title: Packaging as an Interface: CMYK Story Cards & Physical Onboarding
my_role: I designed the onboarding flow and directed the card-based interaction system.
problem: Traditional hardware onboarding requires parents to download an app, scan QR codes, and read paper manuals while kids wait impatiently and lose interest.
context: The unboxing moment sets the emotional baseline for a child's relationship with the product. If setup feels like tech support, the magic disappears.
investigation: Observed family unboxings across multiple competitors. Evaluated card stock thicknesses, matte vs gloss laminations, CMYK color reproduction, and NFC/RFID card integration.
people: I worked with our print vendor and graphic designer.
hypotheses: Physical cards acting as 'content cartridges' bridge the physical and digital worlds for kids without screens.
Rigid unboxing trays that hold the device upright create an immediate 'first awakening' moment.
action: Turned the packaging into an active component of the product. Included durable, heavyweight 400gsm matte-laminated story cards printed in vivid CMYK that act as tangible adventure prompts. Structured the box opening so the device greets the child the moment the lid lifts.
result: First-time setup time dropped to under 90 seconds. Children immediately engaged with the cards as tangible toys before the device was even turned on.
principle: The box basically became another interface. Packaging is not just protection; it is the first chapter of the product experience.
next_time: Finalize card die-lines earlier to avoid rush proofing charges with packaging printers.
why_decision_made: Elevated the perceived value of the product and eliminated parental friction during initial setup.
technical_depth: Paper grain orientation, CMYK color profiles, die-cutting tolerances, matte velvet lamination scuff-resistance, and structural cardboard drop-test testing.
product_thinking: Physical onboarding creates emotional attachment. Making content tangible makes software feel valuable.
business_impact: Significantly reduced return rates during initial trial cohorts by eliminating setup abandonment.
cross_functional_work: Managed print vendor color proofs, die-cut tolerances, and packaging assembly lines simultaneously.
one_line_takeaway: The box basically became another interface. Physical cards turn abstract AI into tangible play.

title: Orchestrating Tooling Vendors & Firmware Under Manufacturing Deadlines
my_role: I acted as the central hub connecting industrial design, tooling shop, and firmware engineers.
problem: Tooling fabricators needed final button travel clearances locked in steel, while the firmware team was still calibrating tactile switch debounce timings.
context: Once injection mold steel is cut, modifying button travel distance costs weeks of downtime. Miscommunication between mechanical and software teams leads to sticky buttons or missed clicks.
investigation: Created an integrated tolerance stack-up sheet mapping switch actuation height, silicone membrane travel, and outer plastic keycap clearance.
people: I worked directly between the mold maker, firmware developer, and mechanical designer.
hypotheses: A shared 0.15mm tolerance buffer will accommodate batch-to-batch switch variation without requiring steel re-work.
action: Set up a unified physical-digital spec sheet. Organized a real-time alignment review with physical test jigs before authorizing T1 mold trials.
result: T1 prototype buttons actuated with crisp, reliable clicks on the first shot. Firmware debounce parameters matched physical tolerances with zero steel modifications.
principle: Small part. Surprisingly large conversation. Cross-functional leadership is about catching misalignment before it gets hardened into steel.
next_time: Establish the tolerance stack-up template as a required milestone before initial tooling kickoff.
why_decision_made: Prevented costly tooling rework and kept production timeline on schedule.
technical_depth: Tolerance stack-up analysis, injection molding shrinkage factors, silicone keypad durometer consistency, and firmware interrupt timing.
product_thinking: The user only feels 'quality' when mechanical travel and software response are perfectly synchronized.
business_impact: Kept the production schedule on track and protected project capital from scrap tooling iterations.
cross_functional_work: Translated firmware latency constraints into mechanical millimeters for toolmakers.
one_line_takeaway: Small part. Surprisingly large conversation. Alignment is cheap; cutting steel twice is expensive.

title: Architecting Sub-800ms Voice Latency for Conversational Language Practice
my_role: I architected the conversational pipeline and benchmarked latency bottlenecks.
problem: Early prototypes had a 2.4-second response lag between user speech end and AI voice output, destroying conversational immersion and making language learners self-conscious.
context: Human conversational turn-taking happens in 200–500ms. In language learning, any pause longer than 1 second causes users to assume the system failed or broke.
investigation: Instrumented end-to-end telemetry across every pipeline phase: Voice Activity Detection (VAD) silence threshold, ASR transcription streaming, LLM Time-to-First-Token (TTFT), and Text-to-Speech (TTS) first-chunk synthesis.
people: I led the technical architecture and worked with backend engineers.
hypotheses: Waiting for complete sentences before sending text to TTS creates unnecessary compounding latency.
Aggressive VAD silence windows (300ms vs 800ms) can cut response initiation without cutting off hesitant speakers.
action: Replaced batch REST endpoints with full-duplex WebSocket streaming. Implemented clause-boundary token chunking so TTS synthesis starts on the very first 4-5 words of the LLM response while generation continues.
result: Turn latency plummeted from 2,400ms to ~780ms. Usability ratings surged as conversation flowed with natural rhythm.
principle: Latency is a product feature, not an infrastructure detail. When you stream the beginning, the middle takes care of itself.
next_time: Build real-time latency telemetry dashboards into the internal test harness from day one.
why_decision_made: A conversational partner must respond quickly to build psychological safety for hesitant language learners.
technical_depth: WebSocket streaming, VAD energy thresholding, LLM streaming output buffers, audio codec transcoding (Opus), and distributed TTS pipelines.
product_thinking: Optimizing for perceptual latency over complete computational completion.
business_impact: Directly unlocked student retention and enabled viable commercial pilot conversations.
cross_functional_work: Synthesized pedagogical requirements with low-level network protocol optimizations.
one_line_takeaway: Latency is the primary UX of voice AI. Stream early words; human brains forgive minor pauses later.

title: RAG Knowledge System: Slashing Latency by ~800× with Semantic Redis Caching
my_role: I designed the end-to-end RAG pipeline and caching strategy.
problem: Querying an 18-volume historical text dataset during live storytelling workshops was generating high API costs and unpredictable response latency (3–6 seconds per query).
context: In live workshop settings, participants ask overlapping semantic questions. Paying for repeated vector search and full LLM generation is financially wasteful and ruins pacing.
investigation: Analyzed query distribution patterns and noticed that ~60% of participant questions clustered around identical themes and character relationships.
people: I built the system and tested it in live dialogue sessions.
hypotheses: Embedding-based semantic caching can intercept near-duplicate queries before touching the LLM.
Tiered caching (exact hash + vector cosine similarity threshold) can preserve factual grounding while eliminating redundant inference.
action: Implemented a dual-layer caching architecture using Redis. Stored pre-computed response embeddings with a strict 0.92 cosine similarity gate for cache hits, falling back to grounded vector search only on novel queries.
result: Achieved ~800× latency reduction (<15ms cache response vs 3,500ms API roundtrip) on repeated queries and eliminated 100% of LLM inference costs for recurring topics.
principle: The fastest and cheapest LLM call is the one you never make. Caching is a core intelligence layer.
next_time: Add proactive cache warming for predictable event themes prior to live sessions.
why_decision_made: Made the application financially sustainable and rock-solid during high-concurrency live demonstrations.
technical_depth: Vector embeddings, Redis caching, cosine similarity metrics, chunking heuristics, and grounded generation guardrails.
product_thinking: High-tier engineering should serve financial viability and operational reliability.
business_impact: Eliminated server cost spikes and enabled real-time conversational workshop performance.
cross_functional_work: Bridged literary humanities research with high-performance database engineering.
one_line_takeaway: The cheapest and fastest LLM call is the one you never make. Caching is an intelligence layer.

title: GyroLens: Physicalizing Motion and Optical Convergence into Pure Discovery
my_role: I conceptualized the physical exhibit, prototyped the optics, and led fabrication.
problem: Rotational mechanics and optical focal convergence are taught as dry formulas in textbooks. Students struggle to develop physical intuition for how light behaves through moving media.
context: At Param Science Experience Centre, exhibits must survive hundreds of thousands of hands while communicating profound physics without walls of instructional text.
investigation: Tested different convex lens curvatures, focal lengths, rotational bearing types, and motorized vs hand-spun momentum systems.
people: I worked with mechanical fabricators, optical specialists, and science educators.
hypotheses: Coupling rotational motion with a centered convex lens creates an emergent 'infinity' pattern that sparks curiosity immediately.
The exhibit must be self-explanatory: the physical affordance alone should invite spinning.
action: Designed and built GyroLens—a custom physical installation combining a precision-balanced rotating gyroscope with a centrally mounted optical lens and aligned directional beam.
result: Became the flagship installation of the House of Glass gallery. Visitors intuitively engaged without reading manuals, repeatedly experimenting with angular speed to watch focal patterns shift.
principle: Rather than explaining the science, let users discover it. If an interface requires an instruction plaque, the design hasn't finished yet.
next_time: Design modular bearing replacement cartridges into the base assembly to simplify ongoing facility maintenance.
why_decision_made: Created lasting educational retention through kinesthetic and visual delight rather than didactic explanation.
technical_depth: Optical focal length calculations, gyroscope precession physics, bearing load ratings, and public-grade durability engineering.
product_thinking: Zero-manual onboarding in the physical world. Affordance is the user manual.
business_impact: Consistently ranked as the highest-dwell-time exhibit in the gallery, generating extensive organic visitor word-of-mouth.
cross_functional_work: Orchestrated precision machinists, glass blowers, electrical lighting contractors, and pedagogical consultants.
one_line_takeaway: If a physical interface requires an instruction plaque, the design hasn't finished yet.

title: Inside the Algorithm: A One-Week Delivery Immersion in Last-Mile Logistics
my_role: I worked as a registered delivery partner on the ground to research system mechanics firsthand.
problem: Product teams sitting in air-conditioned offices design delivery apps assuming ideal conditions, missing the real stress, safety hazards, and micro-incentive gaming that happen in the street.
context: Platforms like Zomato manage millions of human nodes. UX decisions directly dictate road safety, partner earnings, restaurant delays, and customer trust.
investigation: Logged 40+ delivery shifts across peak lunch and dinner hours in Bangalore. Documented every system touchpoint: order stacking, restaurant wait times, GPS drift, gamification badges, and payout logic.
people: Interviewed fellow delivery partners, restaurant dispatchers, and apartment security guards.
hypotheses: The app acts less like a delivery tool and more like an operations gamification engine.
Asymmetry exists: delivery workers are heavily rated and audited, but restaurant hygiene and preparation delays are largely opaque to the system.
action: Synthesized field observations into a comprehensive systems analysis highlighting cognitive load during driving, sound cue recognition, and structural trust gaps between restaurants and delivery workers.
result: Published a widely shared systems case study outlining actionable improvements: restaurant hygiene verification signals, audio-only driving mode, and fair wait-time compensations.
principle: You cannot design systems you refuse to stand inside. Proximity sharpens product judgment faster than analytics dashboards.
next_time: Wear a body camera to capture real-time ambient noise levels during peak traffic navigation.
why_decision_made: Direct field immersion destroys comfortable product assumptions and exposes raw operational truth.
technical_depth: Algorithmic dispatch logic, incentive feedback loops, telemetry accuracy under GPS shadow, and behavioral economics.
product_thinking: Every metric optimized on a dashboard has a human consequence at the end of the line.
business_impact: Demonstrated how grounded field research uncovers high-leverage product opportunities that automated analytics miss.
cross_functional_work: Connected software platform algorithms with human behavioral street realities.
one_line_takeaway: You cannot design systems you refuse to stand inside. Proximity sharpens product judgment.
